extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate public interested in manners, satire, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: A set of Spectator-style essays commenting on contemporary social customs (duelling, fashions, types of persons) and giving moral, practical, and satirical judgments. The page models how to evaluate and ridicule social behaviours in an early-18th-century periodical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duelling is irrational and dishonourable
rubrics_metrics.description: This resentment neither has its foundation from true reason, nor solid fame; but is an imposture, made up of cowardice, falsehood, and want of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues duels are founded on false notions of honour: they often reward folly, enable coxcombs, and lead brave men to unnecessary death while excusing knaves. Use historical examples to show best practices of other ages and nations and treat the custom with humour to persuade the public away from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'giving a man satisfaction' in the contemporary sense
rubrics_metrics.description: By this means it is called, 'giving a man satisfaction,' to urge your offence against him with your sword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase is satirically unpacked by translating a challenge into plain English to show its absurdity: a morning note promising to 'give satisfaction' after a night's insult effectively asks the recipient to risk death for wounded pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to give advice to those who consult you after deciding
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people will ask counsel of you, when they have already acted what they tell you is still under deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asked counsel by someone already decided, the efficient (and socially expedient) tactic is to tell them the opinion they desire: be very clear and positive, leave no handle for scruple, and thus gratify their inclination while appearing to commend their wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to judge a man's character by his household and conduct (Paulo vs Avaro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paulo's habitation has the air of a nobleman and a merchant: servants act with affection; master meets you with an open countenance; business is despatched with confidence; table is the image of plenty and generosity supported by justice and frugality. Avaro has a suspicious aspect, seems to believe visitors thieves, and lives like a beggar though wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable signs—servants' behaviour, hospitality, openness of countenance, fairness in dealings, and visible generosity—to distinguish an honest, civic-minded merchant (Paulo) from a mean-spirited, avaricious one (Avaro) who gains at others' expense. Prefer the former as a model for raising a son.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical classification of fashionable social types ('pretty fellows', 'smart fellows')
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain outward habits and affectations (names called in company, effeminate airs, signs and tokens, receiving visits in bed, nightcap-wigs, red-heeled shoes, not paying at the playhouse, hanging cane on button) identify social classes like 'pretty fellows' or 'smart fellows.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper offers a satirical taxonomy: these fashions and rituals are diagnostic. Enforce or exclude persons in clubs/coffee-houses according to these signs; the classification is both social satire and a guide to whom to admit into genteel circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and moral evaluation of a 'Rake'
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rake is a man always to be pitied; his faults proceed not from choice but from strong passions and appetites—he sins and repents repeatedly, has natural good qualities, and is often imitated to bad effect; to be a rake he must be vicious against his will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the rake with pity rather than mere condemnation. Recognise that his vices stem from temperament and passion; his imitators (second‑hand vice) are particularly pernicious. Distinguish true rakes from mere affecters who lack the underlying disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a coquette
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rake among men is a misuse of reason, a coquette among women lives in continual misapplication of her beauty: affectations (lisping, poring with eyes half shut, giggling at service) disfigure natural charms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify coquetry by habitual artificial behaviors that undermine natural gifts. The coquette secures attention by contrivance rather than sincere merits; such affectations are satirical targets and markers of bad taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship strategy: imitate the parrot (be persistent and vocal)
rubrics_metrics.description: For he who would be loved by women, must never be silent before the favour, or open his lips after it. The parrot in the poetical epistle is held up as the bird of love: to succeed one must be a parrot; to preserve conquests, a dove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical romantic advice in satirical form: persistence and continued vocal expression of affection win courtship; silence after success preserves the conquest (dove symbolism). The injunction is exaggerated for comic effect but functions as an evaluative rule for suitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion strategy for reforming popular but harmful customs
rubrics_metrics.description: You must treat this custom with humour and raillery to get an audience, before you come to pronounce sentence upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing deeply embedded, tragic or senseless customs (e.g., duelling), begin with satire and lightness to engage the public; follow with moral argument and illustrative examples once you have their attention. Lists of typical participants (to expose them to ridicule) are effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think and inquire before risking life or estate (Socratic admonition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Could a man that would not give his estate without reading the instrument, dispose of his life without asking a question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Socratic questioning to show the folly of hasty, honor-driven acts. Before consenting to dangerous undertakings (acting as principal or second in a duel), one should examine motives and consequences; the comparison to reading a will highlights reckless inconsideration.
